# Proof Techniques for Algorithms {#sec-proofs}

::: {.callout-note title="Sources"}
**CLRS** §2.1 (loop invariants), ch. 15 (greedy algorithms, exchange arguments) and 3rd ed. §16.4 (matroids), §8.1 (sorting lower bound), §9.1 (minimum and maximum) · **Erickson** *Algorithms* ch. 1 (induction and recursion), ch. 4 (greedy algorithms, "greedy stays ahead") · **Kleinberg–Tardos** ch. 4 (greedy proofs) · **Knuth** TAOCP vol. 3 §5.3.3 (selection lower bounds) · **CPH** ch. 6 (greedy), ch. 25 (game theory).

**Coverage:** specifications, partial and total correctness · loop invariants and variant functions · weak, strong and structural induction, strengthening the hypothesis · correctness of recursion, DP and game positions · greedy proofs (stays ahead, exchange, matroids) and disproving greedy with counterexamples · contradiction, the extremal principle, pigeonhole · lower bounds (decision trees, information theory, adversaries, reductions) · invariants and monovariants of processes · common proof errors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"}
- State a loop invariant for any loop you write, and use it to prove the loop correct and terminating.
- Prove recursive, DP and game-theory solutions correct by induction, including when you must strengthen the claim.
- Prove a greedy algorithm optimal with an exchange argument or "greedy stays ahead", and break a wrong greedy with a small counterexample.
- Use contradiction, extremal choice and the pigeonhole principle to show that something exists, or to cut a search space in half.
- Prove lower bounds with decision trees and adversary arguments, and know the tight bounds for sorting, min-max and second-largest.
- Find invariants and monovariants of a process to decide what is reachable and whether it terminates.
:::

## Why this matters

::: {.callout-note title="First time writing a proof about code? Read this line first"}
A "proof" in this chapter is not a wall of Greek symbols — it is just a *short, honest reason* why your program is always right, spelled out clearly enough that no hidden test case can argue with it. You do not need to master the formalism to use these ideas. Read each technique once, then run the code cells and watch the claim come true; come back to any section when a later chapter leans on it.
:::

Think about the most expensive bug you can ship: an algorithm that passes every sample you try and then collapses on a hidden test, or falls apart the instant an interviewer asks "but are you sure?" Without a proof you only find out *after* the "Wrong answer on test 37" verdict — and by then it is too late. A proof is simply how you find out *before* that. You do not need formal proofs for every line of code; you just need the habit of asking three questions:

1. **What stays true** every time the loop goes round? (the invariant)
2. **Why does it stop**, and why is the answer right when it stops? (termination)
3. **Why is the choice I make safe?** (greedy and pruning arguments)

Notice that interviewers ask precisely these three questions: "Why does your greedy work?", "Why does this binary search terminate?", "Can you do better than $O(n\log n)$?" The last one is really a question about **lower bounds**, and this chapter covers those too.

Here is the reassuring part: the techniques are few, and once you own them they turn up in every later chapter. This is the whole map:

| Technique | Typical use | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Loop invariant + variant | Loops, binary search, two pointers, partitioning | @sec-pf-invariants |
| Induction | Recursion, DP, games, structural properties of trees | @sec-pf-induction |
| Exchange / stays ahead | Greedy algorithms | @sec-pf-greedy |
| Contradiction, extremal, pigeonhole | Existence, "the answer lies in this half" | @sec-pf-contradiction |
| Decision trees, adversaries | Lower bounds: "you cannot do better" | @sec-pf-lower-bounds |
| Invariants of a process | Reachability, impossibility, termination | @sec-pf-process |

## Correctness: what we are proving {#sec-pf-correctness}

Before we prove anything, we have to be honest about *what* we are proving. An algorithm is never "correct" on its own — only correct *with respect to a specification*, which comes in two halves: a **precondition** (what we are allowed to assume about the input) and a **postcondition** (what must be true about the output). Take binary search for the first position $p$ with $a_p \ge x$:

- *Precondition:* $a$ is sorted in non-decreasing order.
- *Postcondition:* $0 \le p \le n$, every $a_i$ with $i < p$ is $< x$, and every $a_i$ with $i \ge p$ is $\ge x$.

The precondition is not fine print — it *is* the deal. Run the same code on an unsorted array and it returns garbage, yet that is not a "bug," because the code never promised to work there.

Now split correctness into two separate promises, because they need two separate arguments:

- **Partial correctness:** *if* the algorithm stops, the output satisfies the postcondition.
- **Termination:** the algorithm always stops.

**Total correctness** is simply partial correctness *plus* termination. We keep them apart for a reason: a loop like `while True: pass` is vacuously partially correct for *every* specification, because it never stops long enough to be checked. So "the answer is right" and "the program ever finishes" are genuinely two different things to prove.

## Loop invariants {#sec-pf-invariants}

::: {.callout-important title="Loop invariant method"}
A **loop invariant** is a statement $I$ about the program's variables that is true before every iteration of the loop. To prove a loop correct, show:

1. **Initialisation:** $I$ holds before the first iteration.
2. **Maintenance:** if $I$ holds before an iteration (and the loop condition is true), it holds after it.
3. **Termination:** when the loop exits, $I$ together with the negated loop condition implies the postcondition.

To prove the loop **stops**, give a **variant** (also called a ranking function): an integer quantity that is bounded below and strictly decreases every iteration.
:::

If that feels like a lot of ceremony, notice what it really is: plain induction on the iteration count. Step 1 is the base case, step 2 is the inductive step, and step 3 turns "true at every single iteration" into "true the moment the loop finishes" — which is exactly the answer we were after.

### Choosing the invariant

Here is the trick that makes invariants easy to *find* instead of guess: the invariant is almost always the postcondition with one quantity **relaxed**, and the quantity to relax is usually "how far I have gotten." Insertion sort's postcondition is "$a[0..n)$ is sorted"; relax $n$ to the loop counter $i$ and the invariant writes itself: "$a[0..i)$ is sorted, and is just a rearrangement of the original first $i$ elements." The same single relaxation produces the rest of the common loops:

| Loop | Postcondition | Invariant (relaxed) |
|---|---|---|
| Sum / max of an array | `best` = max of $a[0..n)$ | `best` = max of $a[0..i)$ |
| Insertion sort | $a[0..n)$ sorted | $a[0..i)$ sorted |
| Binary search | boundary is at `lo` | $a[<lo] < x \le a[\ge hi]$, boundary in $[lo, hi]$ |
| Partition / Dutch flag | $a$ = all 0s, all 1s, all 2s | three known regions + one unknown region |
| Two pointers on sorted array | found pair or none exists | no pair uses an index outside $[lo, hi]$ |
| Euclid's gcd | `a` = gcd of input | $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(a_0, b_0)$ |

### Worked example 1: Euclid's algorithm

```python
def gcd(a, b):
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a
```

*Invariant:* $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(a_0, b_0)$. **Initialisation**: trivially. **Maintenance**: any common divisor of $a$ and $b$ divides $a \bmod b = a - \lfloor a/b\rfloor b$, and any common divisor of $b$ and $a \bmod b$ divides $a$; so the set of common divisors, and its maximum, are unchanged. **Termination**: when $b = 0$, $\gcd(a, 0) = a$. *Variant:* $b$ is a non-negative integer and $a \bmod b < b$, so $b$ strictly decreases.

Push the same idea one step further and the *running time comes free*: the variant is not merely shrinking, it halves every two steps (if $b \le a/2$ then $a \bmod b < b \le a/2$; otherwise $a \bmod b = a - b < a/2$). So Euclid finishes in $O(\log \min(a, b))$ iterations.

::: {#fig-pf-euclid}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
steps = [(252, 105)]
while steps[-1][1]:
    a_, b_ = steps[-1]
    steps.append((b_, a_ % b_))
assert all(math.gcd(*s) == 21 for s in steps) and steps[-1] == (21, 0)
def draw(ax, p):
    rows = [[str(a_) for a_, _ in steps], [str(b_) for _, b_ in steps], [str(math.gcd(*s)) for s in steps]]
    colors = {(2, c): "green" for c in range(len(steps))}
    colors[(1, len(steps) - 1)] = "amber"
    V.grid(ax, p, rows, row_labels=["a", "b", "gcd(a, b)"], col_labels=[f"step {i}" for i in range(len(steps))],
           colors=colors, cell_w=1.4)
V.show(draw)
```

Euclid on (252, 105). Each step replaces (a, b) by (b, a mod b); the gcd of the pair never changes (the invariant) and b strictly shrinks (the variant) until it reaches 0.

:::

### Worked example 2: insertion sort

```{python}
#| label: pf-insertion
def insertion_sort_checked(a):
    a = list(a)
    original = list(a)
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        # Invariant at the top of iteration i: a[:i] is sorted and is a permutation of original[:i]
        assert all(a[k] <= a[k + 1] for k in range(i - 1)) and sorted(a[:i]) == sorted(original[:i])
        if i == len(a):
            break
        j, x = i, a[i]
        while j > 0 and a[j - 1] > x:
            a[j] = a[j - 1]
            j -= 1
        a[j] = x
    return a

for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 15))]
    assert insertion_sort_checked(a) == sorted(a)
```

::: {#fig-pf-insertion}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    a = [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]
    rows = []
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        rows.append(dict(values=list(a), regions=[(0, i, "green", "")],
                         colors={i: "amber"} if i < len(a) else {}, index=False, label=f"i = {i}"))
        assert a[:i] == sorted(a[:i])
        if i < len(a):
            x, j = a[i], i
            while j > 0 and a[j - 1] > x:
                a[j] = a[j - 1]; j -= 1
            a[j] = x
    V.trace(ax, p, rows, gap=1.4)
V.show(draw)
```

Insertion sort on [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]. At the top of each iteration the green prefix a[:i] is sorted (the invariant); the amber element is the one being inserted next.

:::

There is a wonderfully practical shortcut hiding here: write the invariant as an `assert` *inside* the loop, exactly as the cell above does. If a stress test over random inputs never trips it, the invariant is at least believable; and if it does trip, the failing iteration tells you precisely where your reasoning went wrong — which is far more useful than a wrong answer with no clue.

### Worked example 3: a loop that does not terminate

```python
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if ok(mid): lo = mid      # bug
    else:       hi = mid - 1
```

Where is the flaw? The variant $hi - lo$ has to *strictly decrease*, and here it does not. With $lo = 4$, $hi = 5$ we get $mid = 4$; if `ok(4)` holds we set `lo = 4` once more, the window never shrinks, and the loop spins forever. The fix is to round $mid$ **up** whenever the branch that keeps $mid$ is the one assigning `lo = mid`: `mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2`. The rule worth memorising: whichever side is allowed to *keep* `mid` must not be the side `mid` naturally rounds toward.

::: {#fig-pf-stuck}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    vals = ["", "", "", "", "T", "?", "", ""]
    for r in range(3):
        V.array(ax, p, vals, 0, -r * 2.6, index=r == 0, dim=[0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7],
                regions=[(4, 6, "pink", "")], pointers=[(4, "lo = mid", "indigo")], label=f"round {r + 1}")
    V.text(ax, p, 9.2, -2.1, "no progress:\nhi − lo stays 1", ha="left", color="pink")
V.show(draw)
```

The non-terminating binary search: with lo = 4, hi = 5, mid rounds down to 4, ok(4) sets lo = 4 again, and the window never shrinks. Rounding mid up (mid = 5) fixes it.

:::

## Induction {#sec-pf-induction}

::: {.callout-important title="Forms of induction"}
- **Weak induction:** prove $P(0)$, and $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)$.
- **Strong induction:** prove $P(n)$ assuming $P(k)$ for **all** $k < n$ (base cases included as needed).
- **Structural induction:** prove $P$ for the smallest structures (empty tree, single node), and prove it for a structure assuming it for its parts (subtrees, sublists).
:::

Of these, **strong induction** is the one algorithms actually run on. A recursive call may hand back *any* smaller size, not just $n-1$, and strong induction is exactly the version whose hypothesis already covers every smaller case — which is why it lines up so naturally with recursion.

### Recursion is induction

To prove a recursive function correct:

1. **Base cases** return the right answer.
2. Assuming every recursive call (on a strictly smaller input) returns the right answer, the function combines them into the right answer.
3. Every call is on a **strictly smaller** input in some well-founded order, so the recursion terminates.

Read those three lines again and you will see it is just strong induction on the input size wearing a different hat. This is also why experienced people never trace a recursive function more than one level deep: you *assume* the smaller calls are correct (that is the hypothesis) and check only that the current call combines them correctly.

### DP correctness is induction on the state order

A dynamic program is really just induction stored in a table, so its proof has the same two ingredients. First, the recurrence must be right: the best answer for a state comes from best answers of smaller states (**optimal substructure**). Second, the states must be filled in an order where every dependency is ready before you need it. Feed those two facts through strong induction on that order and *every* table entry is correct. A habit that pays off: when you design a DP, say the recurrence out loud as a claim — "$dp[i]$ = the best value over all … ending at $i$" — because that one sentence *is* your induction hypothesis.

### Strengthening the hypothesis

This next idea rescues induction more often than anything else, so it is worth internalising. Sometimes $P(n)$ is simply too weak to carry you to $P(n+1)$ — yet a *stronger*, more detailed statement sails straight through. The classic toy example is proving $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{i^2} < 2$. Try induction directly and it stalls: knowing the sum is "$< 2$" tells you nothing once you add $\frac1{(n+1)^2}$, since it could already be sitting at $1.999\ldots$ with no room left. The fix is to *strengthen* the claim to the sharper $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac1{i^2} \le 2 - \frac1n$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&2 - \frac1n + \frac{1}{(n+1)^2} \le 2 - \frac{1}{n+1} \\
\iff{} &\frac{1}{(n+1)^2} \le \frac1n - \frac1{n+1} = \frac{1}{n(n+1)},
\end{aligned}
$$
which is plainly true. This is not a number trick — the very same move shows up constantly in real code. A tree DFS that only "returns the height" cannot tell you whether the tree is balanced, because height alone is the wrong quantity to induct on; but a DFS that returns the *stronger* pair "(is balanced, height)" for each subtree glues together perfectly.

::: {#fig-pf-strengthen}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
ns = list(range(1, 41))
partial, acc = [], 0.0
for n in ns:
    acc += 1.0 / n**2
    partial.append(acc)
top = [2 - 1.0 / n for n in ns]
def draw(ax, p):
    ax.plot(ns, partial, color=p["indigo"], lw=2, marker="o", ms=3, label=r"partial sum $\sum 1/i^2$")
    ax.plot(ns, top, color=p["green"], lw=2, ls="--", label=r"sharper bound $2 - 1/n$")
    ax.axhline(2, color=p["red"], lw=1.5, ls=":", label=r"weak bound $2$")
    ax.set_xlabel("n"); ax.set_ylabel("sum"); ax.set_ylim(0.8, 2.15); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
V.plot(draw)
```

The weak bound (red) is exactly what plain induction cannot step across, because the running sum crowds up against it. The strengthened bound (green) always leaves the sum a full $1/n$ of headroom, so the inductive step goes through — while still implying the original claim.

:::

### The broken induction

Why be so careful? Because a proof can look airtight and still be wrong. The notorious "all horses are the same colour" fake-proof runs like this: for $n = 1$ it is obviously true; assume any $n$ horses share one colour; then in a group of $n+1$ horses the first $n$ share a colour and the last $n$ share a colour, and since the two groups overlap, surely all $n+1$ match. The flaw is sneaky and tiny: when $n + 1 = 2$ the two groups $\{h_1\}$ and $\{h_2\}$ **do not overlap at all**, so the very first step $P(1) \Rightarrow P(2)$ is false. The lesson to keep: always check that your inductive step genuinely works for the **smallest** case where you apply it, not just for large $n$.

```{python}
#| label: pf-strengthen
# The strengthened bound holds, and is tight enough to imply the original one.
s = 0.0
for n in range(1, 10**5 + 1):
    s += 1 / n**2
    assert s <= 2 - 1 / n + 1e-12
print(f"sum to 1e5 = {s:.6f}  (limit pi^2/6 = {math.pi**2 / 6:.6f})")
```

## Greedy proofs {#sec-pf-greedy}

A greedy algorithm is at once the most tempting and the most treacherous design you will use: it builds an answer by taking the locally best choice at every step and *never* looking back. That makes it fast and short to write — and just as easy to get subtly wrong, because "best so far" all too often fails to be "best overall." Happily, almost every correct greedy is proved with one of just two templates:

::: {.callout-important title="Two templates for greedy proofs"}
**Greedy stays ahead.** Measure progress after $k$ steps. Show by induction that after every step, the greedy solution is at least as far ahead as any other solution. Then show that being ahead at the end means being optimal.

**Exchange argument.** Take any optimal solution $O$ that differs from the greedy solution $G$. Find the first place they differ and **swap** $O$'s choice for $G$'s. Show the swap keeps $O$ feasible and does not make it worse. Repeating the swap turns $O$ into $G$ without loss, so $G$ is optimal.
:::

### Worked example: activity selection

Choose the maximum number of pairwise non-overlapping intervals. Greedy: sort by **end time**, take each interval that starts no earlier than the end of the last one taken.

*Greedy stays ahead.* Let $g_1, g_2, \dots, g_k$ be the greedy intervals and $o_1, \dots, o_m$ any valid solution, both sorted by end. **Claim:** $\text{end}(g_i) \le \text{end}(o_i)$ for every $i \le \min(k, m)$. For $i = 1$, greedy picked the interval with the smallest end overall. If $\text{end}(g_{i-1}) \le \text{end}(o_{i-1}) \le \text{start}(o_i)$, then $o_i$ was still available to greedy at step $i$, so greedy chose something ending no later. Now if $m > k$, the interval $o_{k+1}$ starts after $\text{end}(o_k) \ge \text{end}(g_k)$, so greedy would have taken it — contradiction. So $k \ge m$.

::: {#fig-pf-activity}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
acts = [(1, 4, "a"), (3, 5, "b"), (0, 6, "c"), (5, 7, "d"), (3, 9, "e"), (5, 9, "f"), (6, 10, "g"), (8, 11, "h")]
chosen, last = [], -math.inf
for s, e, name in sorted(acts, key=lambda t: t[1]):
    if s >= last:
        chosen.append(name); last = e
assert chosen == ["a", "d", "h"]
# No larger compatible set exists (brute force over all subsets of the 8 activities).
best = max(len(sub) for k in range(len(acts) + 1) for sub in combinations(sorted(acts, key=lambda t: t[1]), k)
           if all(sub[i][1] <= sub[i + 1][0] for i in range(len(sub) - 1)))
assert best == len(chosen)
def draw(ax, p):
    items = [(s, e, name, "green" if name in chosen else "muted", name not in chosen)
             for s, e, name in sorted(acts, key=lambda t: t[1])]
    V.intervals(ax, p, items, row_h=0.6)
V.show(draw)
```

Greedy by end time keeps the green intervals: each one ends no later than the corresponding interval of any other valid choice, so greedy is never behind.

:::

It is tempting to assume any sensible ordering works, but "sort by start" and "sort by length" both fail here, and small hand-drawn counterexamples expose them at once (you will build one in exercise 6).

### Disproving a greedy: search for a counterexample

So how do you catch a greedy that is *wrong* before an interviewer or a hacker does? The fastest way by far is to pit it against a brute force on many small random inputs and watch for a single disagreement. The textbook case is making change with coins $\{1, 3, 4\}$: greedy grabs the biggest coin that fits and pays 6 as $4 + 1 + 1$ (three coins), yet $3 + 3$ does it in two. No amount of "it looks right" survives that test.

```{python}
#| label: pf-coin-counterexample
def greedy_coins(coins, x):
    count = 0
    for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):
        count += x // c
        x %= c
    return count if x == 0 else math.inf

def optimal_coins(coins, x):
    best = [0] + [math.inf] * x
    for v in range(1, x + 1):
        best[v] = min((best[v - c] + 1 for c in coins if c <= v), default=math.inf)
    return best[x]

def first_counterexample(coins, limit=200):
    return next((x for x in range(1, limit) if greedy_coins(coins, x) != optimal_coins(coins, x)), None)

assert first_counterexample([1, 3, 4]) == 6
assert first_counterexample([1, 5, 10, 25]) is None           # US coins: greedy is optimal
assert first_counterexample([1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200]) is None
print("coins {1, 7, 10}: first failure at", first_counterexample([1, 7, 10]))
```

::: {#fig-pf-coins}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
assert greedy_coins([1, 3, 4], 6) == 3 and optimal_coins([1, 3, 4], 6) == 2
def draw(ax, p):
    V.array(ax, p, [4, 1, 1], index=False, colors={0: "amber", 1: "red", 2: "red"}, label="greedy", note="3 coins")
    V.array(ax, p, [3, 3], 0, -1.6, index=False, colors={0: "green", 1: "green"}, label="optimal", note="2 coins")
V.show(draw)
```

Paying 6 with coins {1, 3, 4}: greedy grabs the 4 and then needs two 1s; the optimum uses two 3s.

:::

Coin systems on which greedy is always optimal even have a name: **canonical**. US and euro denominations are canonical, which is exactly why "just take the biggest coin" feels so natural — but $\{1, 3, 4\}$ and $\{1, 7, 10\}$ are not. There is no rule of thumb you can eyeball to tell the two apart; you either prove it or test it.

### Matroids, briefly

This subsection is optional on a first pass, but it answers a question you may already be feeling: *why* does greedy keep working for some problems and fail for others? The deep reason is a structure called a **matroid**. Greedy is guaranteed optimal for "choose a maximum-weight independent set" whenever the independent sets obey just two rules: (1) subsets of independent sets are independent, and (2) if $|A| < |B|$ are independent, some element of $B \setminus A$ can be added to $A$. Forests of a graph form a matroid (so Kruskal's MST algorithm is correct), and so do linearly independent sets of vectors (the XOR basis of the bits chapter). Interval scheduling, by contrast, is **not** a matroid — which is precisely why it needed its own argument above. CLRS (3rd ed.) §16.4 has the full theory.

## Contradiction, the extremal principle and pigeonhole {#sec-pf-contradiction}

Some facts are hardest to prove by charging straight at them, and far easier by ruling out every alternative. A **proof by contradiction** assumes the claim is *false* and follows the logic until it crashes into something impossible. In algorithms its best companion is the **extremal principle**: rather than hunting for just any object with your property, look at the single *largest*, *smallest*, *first*, or *last* object of a kind, and show that this extreme one is forced to have the property.

- "Every DAG has a vertex with no incoming edges." Take a **longest** path; its first vertex can have no incoming edge (from a vertex on the path, that would be a cycle; from a vertex off the path, the path would be longer).
- "Every finite array has a peak" (an element at least as big as its neighbours). Take the **maximum** element.

The **pigeonhole principle** is the most useful "obvious" idea in all of computing: cram $n + 1$ objects into $n$ boxes and some box is bound to hold at least two. The generalised version is what you actually reach for: $N$ objects into $k$ boxes force at least $\lceil N/k \rceil$ into some box.

- Among any $m + 1$ integers, two are congruent modulo $m$.
- Among the prefix sums $S_0 = 0, S_1, \dots, S_m$ of any $m$ integers, two are congruent modulo $m$; their difference is a non-empty subarray whose sum is divisible by $m$ (@sec-pf-p4-modulo).
- A sequence of $rs + 1$ distinct numbers has an increasing subsequence of length $r + 1$ or a decreasing one of length $s + 1$ (Erdős–Szekeres).

```{python}
#| label: pf-pigeonhole
def divisible_subarray(a):
    """Return (l, r) with sum(a[l:r]) % m == 0, m = len(a). Exists by pigeonhole."""
    m = len(a)
    seen = {0: 0}
    s = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(a, 1):
        s = (s + x) % m
        if s in seen:
            return seen[s], i
        seen[s] = i
    raise AssertionError("pigeonhole guarantees this is unreachable")

for _ in range(1000):
    a = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 20))]
    l, r = divisible_subarray(a)
    assert l < r and sum(a[l:r]) % len(a) == 0
```

::: {#fig-pf-pigeonhole}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
a = [3, 4, 1, 5, 2]
l, r = divisible_subarray(a)
assert (l, r) == (1, 3) and sum(a[l:r]) % 5 == 0
prefix = [0]
for x in a:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + x)
def draw(ax, p):
    rows = [[""] + a, prefix, [s % 5 for s in prefix]]
    colors = {(0, c + 1): "indigo" for c in range(l, r)}
    colors.update({(2, l): "green", (2, r): "green", (1, l): "green", (1, r): "green"})
    V.grid(ax, p, rows, row_labels=["a", "prefix S", "S mod 5"], col_labels=[f"S{i}" for i in range(6)], colors=colors)
V.show(draw)
```

a = [3, 4, 1, 5, 2] with m = 5. The six prefix sums S₀..S₅ take only five residues mod 5, so two must match: S₁ ≡ S₃ ≡ 3, and a[1:3] = [4, 1] sums to 5.

:::

## Lower bounds {#sec-pf-lower-bounds}

Everything so far produced *upper* bounds: "my algorithm needs at most $f(n)$ steps." A **lower bound** makes the opposite and far stronger claim: "*every* algorithm, in some agreed model, needs at least $g(n)$ steps." When an upper and a lower bound meet, the problem is provably solved optimally and you can stop trying to improve it. That is exactly what lets you answer the interview question "can you do better?" with real confidence instead of a guess.

The phrase "in some model" is doing a lot of quiet work: a lower bound is only ever a statement about the operations you *allow* an algorithm to use. The famous $\Omega(n\log n)$ sorting bound holds for **comparison** sorts; counting sort sidesteps it by using array indexing, an operation that simply is not inside that model — so it never contradicts the bound.

### Decision trees and information theory

The cleanest model to reason about is a comparison sort, which you can picture as a binary decision tree: every internal node asks one question of the form "$a_i < a_j$?", its two branches are the yes and no answers, and every leaf is a final ordering. If the problem has $L$ distinct answers the algorithm must be able to tell apart, the tree needs at least $L$ leaves — and a binary tree with $L$ leaves is at least $\lceil\log_2 L\rceil$ tall, which is exactly the worst-case number of comparisons.

| Problem | Possible answers $L$ | Lower bound $\lceil\log_2 L\rceil$ | Matching algorithm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Search a sorted array | $n + 1$ insertion points | $\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$ | binary search |
| Sort $n$ distinct items | $n!$ | $\lceil\log_2 n!\rceil \approx n\log_2 n - 1.44n$ | merge sort ($\le n\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$) |
| Merge two sorted lists of size $n$ | $\binom{2n}{n}$ | $\approx 2n - \frac12\log_2 n$ | standard merge ($2n - 1$) |

```{python}
#| label: pf-sorting-bound
def merge_sort_count(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a, 0
    m = len(a) // 2
    left, cl = merge_sort_count(a[:m])
    right, cr = merge_sort_count(a[m:])
    out, i, j, c = [], 0, 0, cl + cr
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        c += 1
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:], c

# Small n: the exact worst case over all n! inputs can never beat the lower bound.
for n in range(1, 8):
    worst = max(merge_sort_count(list(p))[1] for p in permutations(range(n)))
    lower = math.ceil(math.log2(math.factorial(n)))
    assert lower <= worst <= n * math.ceil(math.log2(max(n, 1)))
    print(f"n={n}  lower bound={lower:3d}  merge sort worst case={worst:3d}")
# Larger n: merge sort stays within n*ceil(log2 n), close to the bound.
for n in [100, 1000]:
    c = merge_sort_count(random.sample(range(n), n))[1]
    print(f"n={n}  lower bound={math.ceil(math.log2(math.factorial(n)))}  one random run={c}")
    assert c <= n * math.ceil(math.log2(n))
```

::: {#fig-pf-decision-tree}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def q(label, yes, no):
    yes.edge, no.edge = "yes", "no"
    return V.Node(label, [yes, no], color="indigo")
def leaf(order):
    return V.Node(order, color="green")
def sort_tree():
    return q("a<b", q("b<c", leaf("abc"), q("a<c", leaf("acb"), leaf("cab"))),
                    q("a<c", leaf("bac"), q("b<c", leaf("bca"), leaf("cba"))))
def walk(v, vals):
    while v.children:
        x, y = v.label.split("<")
        v = v.children[0 if vals[x] < vals[y] else 1]
    return v.label
for perm in permutations([1, 2, 3]):
    vals = dict(zip("abc", perm))
    assert walk(sort_tree(), vals) == "".join(sorted("abc", key=vals.get))
def draw(ax, p):
    V.tree(ax, p, sort_tree(), dx=1.25, dy=1.45)
V.show(draw)
```

A decision tree that sorts three items a, b, c. Each internal node is one comparison; each of the 3! = 6 leaves is an output order. The height is 3 = ⌈log₂ 6⌉, so no comparison sort of 3 items can do better in the worst case.

:::

Counting leaves is powerful but can undershoot. Finding the maximum has just $n$ possible answers, so the information bound gives only $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ — yet the true cost is $n - 1$. Where does the gap come from? Every element other than the maximum must *lose at least one comparison*, or else there would be no way to rule it out as the maximum. That reasoning never counts leaves at all; it is the first flavour of an **adversary argument**.

### Adversary arguments

Turn the tables and let a malicious oracle choose the input *while* your algorithm runs. An **adversary** answers each comparison the moment it is asked, always staying consistent with *some* real input, and its single goal is to keep you as uncertain as possible for as long as possible. If the adversary can force $g(n)$ questions before any answer is pinned down, then *no* algorithm can beat $g(n)$ comparisons in the worst case. Two classic results use exactly this trick, both proved in @sec-pf-p5:

- Finding **both** the minimum and the maximum needs $\lceil 3n/2 \rceil - 2$ comparisons.
- Finding the **second largest** needs $n + \lceil \log_2 n\rceil - 2$ comparisons.

### Reductions

The last tool is borrowing other people's lower bounds. If problem $A$ can be solved using an algorithm for $B$ plus only a little extra work, then any lower bound on $A$ automatically transfers to $B$ — you cannot make $B$ cheap without also making $A$ cheap. **Element distinctness** ("are all $n$ numbers different?") needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ in the algebraic decision-tree model. Closest pair of points in 1D solves it (the closest distance is 0 iff there is a duplicate), so closest pair inherits the same $\Omega(n\log n)$ floor — which is precisely why the $O(n\log n)$ divide-and-conquer algorithm is optimal there. Hashing escapes this bound only because it operates outside the model.

## Invariants of a process {#sec-pf-process}

The invariant instinct is not confined to loops — it is also the sharpest tool for puzzles and "can you reach state $B$ from state $A$ using only these moves?" questions, where the number of reachable states is astronomical but a single clever quantity settles everything. Two kinds of quantity do all the work:

- An **invariant** is a quantity that no move changes (a parity, a sum modulo $k$, a sorted multiset). If the start and target values differ, the target is **unreachable**.
- A **monovariant** is a quantity that every move changes in one direction (strictly decreases, say) and that is bounded. It proves the process **terminates**, and often bounds the number of moves.

Examples:

- A chessboard with two opposite corners removed cannot be tiled by dominoes: each domino covers one black and one white square, but the board has two more of one colour.
- In the 15-puzzle, the parity of (permutation parity + blank's row) is invariant, so half of all configurations are unreachable.
- Bubble sort's swap of an adjacent inverted pair reduces the number of inversions by exactly 1, a monovariant: it terminates after exactly (number of inversions) swaps.

```{python}
#| label: pf-bubble-monovariant
def inversions(a):
    return sum(a[i] > a[j] for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a)))

def bubble_swaps(a):
    a, swaps = list(a), 0
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(a) - 1):
            if a[i] > a[i + 1]:
                before = inversions(a)
                a[i], a[i + 1] = a[i + 1], a[i]
                assert inversions(a) == before - 1          # monovariant drops by exactly 1
                swaps, changed = swaps + 1, True
    return swaps

for _ in range(200):
    a = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 9))]
    assert bubble_swaps(a) == inversions(a)
```

::: {#fig-pf-bubble}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    a, rows = [4, 3, 2, 1], []
    rows.append(dict(values=list(a), index=False, label="start", note=f"{inversions(a)} inversions"))
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(a) - 1):
            if a[i] > a[i + 1]:
                a[i], a[i + 1] = a[i + 1], a[i]
                changed = True
                rows.append(dict(values=list(a), index=False, colors={i: "amber", i + 1: "amber"},
                                 label=f"swap {len(rows)}", note=f"{inversions(a)} inversions"))
    assert len(rows) == 7 and a == [1, 2, 3, 4]
    V.trace(ax, p, rows, gap=1.35)
V.show(draw)
```

Bubble sort on [4, 3, 2, 1]. Every swap of an adjacent inverted pair (amber) removes exactly one inversion, so the number of inversions is a monovariant: 6 swaps, then it must stop.

:::

## Pattern 1: prove the loop with an invariant {#sec-pf-p1}

**Where we are.** The lessons gave you the proof tools. The patterns apply them to claims that reach further each time: one loop (this pattern), every input size $n$ (Pattern 2), a choice compared with every other choice (Pattern 3), an object whose existence is forced (Pattern 4), every possible algorithm at once (Pattern 5), and a whole process of moves (Pattern 6). Each problem in a pattern adds one twist to the one before it.

**Recognise it.** Any loop whose correctness is not obvious: binary search, partitioning, two pointers, in-place rearrangement, "one pass with a candidate".

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
1. Write the postcondition.
2. Relax it into an invariant: the postcondition for the part processed so far, plus what you know about the unprocessed part (regions, pointer bounds).
3. Check initialisation, maintenance (for **each** branch of the loop body), and that invariant + exit condition ⇒ postcondition.
4. Give a variant that strictly decreases (for example $hi - lo$, or the size of the unknown region).
:::

**Complexity.** The variant usually gives the running time too: $hi - lo$ halving means $O(\log n)$; an unknown region shrinking by 1 means $O(n)$.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0035-search-insert-position/problem.qmd >}}

[**From one window to four regions.** Search Insert Position keeps one window and halves it. Sort Colours keeps four regions and shrinks the unknown one by a single element per step, so the invariant has more parts and every branch of the loop must keep all of them.]{.flow-bridge}


::: {#fig-pf-anim-flag}

```{python}
#| echo: false
fl_a = [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]
fl_state = list(fl_a)
lo, mid, hi = 0, 0, len(fl_a) - 1
fl_frames = [(list(fl_state), lo, mid, hi)]
fl_caps = ["start: everything is unknown"]
while mid <= hi:
    x = fl_state[mid]
    if x == 0:
        fl_state[lo], fl_state[mid] = fl_state[mid], fl_state[lo]
        lo += 1; mid += 1
        fl_caps.append("a[mid] = 0: swap it to the 0s, lo and mid move right")
    elif x == 1:
        mid += 1
        fl_caps.append("a[mid] = 1: already in place, mid moves right")
    else:
        fl_state[mid], fl_state[hi] = fl_state[hi], fl_state[mid]
        hi -= 1
        fl_caps.append("a[mid] = 2: swap it to the 2s, hi moves left (the new a[mid] is unknown)")
    fl_frames.append((list(fl_state), lo, mid, hi))
assert fl_state == sorted(fl_a) and len(fl_frames) <= 15

def fl_frame(ax, p, k):
    st, lo, mid, hi = fl_frames[k]
    colors = {i: "green" for i in range(lo)}
    colors.update({i: "cyan" for i in range(lo, mid)})
    colors.update({i: "amber" for i in range(hi + 1, len(st))})
    ptrs = [(lo, "lo", "green"), (hi, "hi", "amber", "top")] if lo != mid else [(lo, "lo = mid", "green"), (hi, "hi", "amber", "top")]
    if lo != mid and mid < len(st):
        ptrs.append((mid, "mid", "indigo"))
    V.array(ax, p, st, colors=colors, pointers=[q for q in ptrs if 0 <= q[0] <= len(st)], cell_w=1.2)

V.animate(fl_frame, len(fl_frames), captions=fl_caps, interval=1100)
del lo, mid, hi, x                # keep the chapter's namespace clean
```

Sort Colours on $[2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]$. Green cells are 0s, cyan 1s, amber 2s, white the unknown region between `mid` and `hi`. Every frame keeps all four regions intact (the invariant) and shrinks the unknown region by one cell (the variant), so the loop ends after $n$ steps with the array sorted.

:::

{{< include ../problems/lc-0075-sort-colors/problem.qmd >}}

[**From where elements sit to how they split.** Both invariants so far describe positions. Boyer–Moore voting never moves anything: its invariant describes how the processed prefix splits into copies of the candidate and cancelled pairs.]{.flow-bridge}


### Majority element: the invariant behind voting {#sec-pf-p1-majority}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0169-majority-element/card.qmd >}}

The hashing chapter solves this problem in full; here we only prove its one-pass voting loop. Keep `cand` and `count`; for each $x$, adopt $x$ when `count == 0`, then add $1$ if $x =$ `cand` and subtract $1$ otherwise.

**Invariant.** After processing a prefix $P$, the elements of $P$ split into (a) `count` copies of `cand` and (b) a set of **disjoint pairs of different values**.

- *Initialisation:* the empty prefix is zero copies and zero pairs.
- *Maintenance:* if $x =$ `cand` (or `count` was $0$ and $x$ was just adopted), $x$ joins part (a). Otherwise $x$ and one copy of `cand` leave part (a) together as a new pair of different values.
- *Termination:* $p$ pairs hold $2p$ elements but at most $p$ copies of the majority value $m$. If every copy of $m$ sat in a pair, $m$ would fill at most half of the array, which contradicts the guarantee. So some copy of $m$ is in part (a), and `cand` $= m$.

::: {#fig-pf-anim-vote}

```{python}
#| echo: false
bm_a = [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
bm_rows, bm_caps, cand, count, pairs = [], [], None, 0, 0
for x in bm_a:
    if count == 0:
        cand = x
        how = f"count was 0: adopt {x}, count 1"
        count = 1
    elif x == cand:
        count += 1
        how = f"{x} = cand: count {count}"
    else:
        count -= 1
        pairs += 1
        how = f"{x} differs from cand {cand}: one pair cancelled, count {count}"
    bm_rows.append((cand, count, pairs))
    bm_caps.append(how + f"; pairs so far {pairs}")
assert cand == 2 and count + 2 * pairs == len(bm_a)

def bm_frame(ax, p, k):
    cands = [str(r[0]) if j <= k else "" for j, r in enumerate(bm_rows)]
    counts = [str(r[1]) if j <= k else "" for j, r in enumerate(bm_rows)]
    colors = {(0, k): "indigo", (2, k): "green" if bm_rows[k][1] else "amber"}
    V.grid(ax, p, [bm_a, cands, counts], row_labels=["a", "cand", "count"], colors=colors, cell_w=1.1)

V.animate(bm_frame, len(bm_a), captions=bm_caps, interval=1100)
del x, cand, count, pairs, how                # keep the chapter's namespace clean
```

Boyer–Moore voting on $[2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]$, one element per frame. After every frame the processed prefix is exactly `count` copies of `cand` plus the cancelled pairs: the caption's two numbers always add up to the prefix length. Amber marks the moment the count reaches $0$ and the next element is adopted.

:::

Without the guarantee the candidate means nothing (on $[1, 2, 3]$ it is $3$), so verify it with a second pass when a majority might not exist. The cell below checks the invariant itself, not just the answer: it keeps the pairs explicitly and asserts the split after every step.

```{python}
#| label: pf-majority
def majority(a):
    cand, count, pairs = None, 0, []
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        if count == 0:
            cand = x
        if x == cand:
            count += 1
        else:
            count -= 1
            pairs.append((x, cand))
        # the invariant: a[:i+1] = count copies of cand + disjoint pairs of different values
        assert all(u != v for u, v in pairs)
        assert Counter(a[:i + 1]) == Counter([cand] * count + [v for pr in pairs for v in pr])
    return cand

for _ in range(1000):
    n = random.randint(1, 20)
    m = random.randint(0, 5)
    k = n // 2 + 1 + random.randint(0, (n - 1) // 2)       # copies of m: strictly more than n/2
    a = [m] * k + [random.choice([v for v in range(6) if v != m]) for _ in range(n - k)]
    random.shuffle(a)
    assert majority(a) == m

assert majority([1, 2, 3]) == 3            # no majority: the candidate means nothing
assert majority([1, 2, 3, 1]) == 3         # 1 has exactly n/2 copies, not more: wrong answer
```

## Pattern 2: induction on the input (recursion, DP, games) {#sec-pf-p2}

**From one loop to every n.** An invariant proves one loop correct. When the claim is about every size $n$, and the answer for $n$ is built from answers for smaller $n$, the same idea becomes induction: the invariant now runs over $n$ instead of over the loop counter.

**Recognise it.** A recursive solution, a DP, or a two-player game where you suspect a pattern (a formula in $n \bmod k$, a parity). The claim is about **every** $n$, and the answer for $n$ depends on answers for smaller $n$.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
1. State the claim $P(n)$ precisely (for games: "position $n$ is winning iff …").
2. Check the base cases.
3. Assume $P(k)$ for all $k < n$ (strong induction). Show $P(n)$ using only the step the algorithm or the game rules take from $n$.
4. Before proving, **compute** $P(n)$ for small $n$ by brute force to find the pattern and to test the claim.
:::

**Complexity.** Not about running time: induction often turns an $O(n)$ DP into an $O(1)$ formula.

For games, the base fact is: a position is **winning** if *some* move leads to a losing position, and **losing** if *every* move leads to a winning position (or there is no move).

{{< include ../problems/lc-0292-nim-game/problem.qmd >}}

[**From fixed moves to moves that depend on n.** In Nim you may always take 1, 2 or 3. In the Divisor Game the legal moves depend on the divisors of $n$, so the induction step reasons about parity instead of a fixed list of moves.]{.flow-bridge}


{{< include ../problems/lc-1025-divisor-game/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a pattern to a pattern that changes.** Both games so far have one pattern for all $n$. In the 1-2-K Game an extra move of size $k$ can change the losing positions, so the claim to prove by induction depends on $k$.]{.flow-bridge}


{{< include ../problems/cf-1194d-1-2-k-game/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 3: prove a greedy choice by exchange {#sec-pf-p3}

**From what happens to what is best.** Induction shows that an algorithm computes what it claims. A greedy algorithm must also beat every other choice, and the exchange argument shows that by turning any optimal solution into the greedy one without making it worse.

**Recognise it.** An optimisation problem where sorting by some key and taking items in order looks plausible: scheduling, interval selection, assignment, pairing.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
1. Guess the sort key, then **test** the greedy against brute force on small random inputs. Most wrong keys die here in seconds.
2. Prove it: take an optimal solution $O$ and the first position where it disagrees with greedy $G$. Swap $O$'s choice for $G$'s and show the result is still feasible and no worse (exchange); or show by induction that $G$ is never behind $O$ (stays ahead).
3. For "sort by a comparison" problems, the exchange usually reduces to comparing **two adjacent** elements: if swapping an adjacent pair that is out of key order never hurts, sorting by the key is optimal.
:::

**Complexity.** Usually $O(n\log n)$ for the sort plus $O(n)$ for the scan.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0435-non-overlapping-intervals/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a sort by a field to a sort by a difference.** Non-overlapping Intervals sorts by a field of the input, the end time. Two City Scheduling must first rewrite the cost (send everyone to B, then switch $n$ people) before the right key, $a_i - b_i$, appears.]{.flow-bridge}


{{< include ../problems/lc-1029-two-city-scheduling/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 4: contradiction, extremal choice and pigeonhole {#sec-pf-p4}

**From building an answer to proving one exists.** The patterns so far proved that a construction is right. Sometimes it is enough to prove that an answer *exists* in some part of the input. That proof, by contradiction, by an extremal choice or by pigeonhole, tells you which half to search, or that you can stop at once.

**Recognise it.** You need to show that something **exists** (a peak, a duplicate, a subarray with a property), or to decide which **half** of a search space must contain it. Often the existence proof directly gives a binary search or an $O(1)$ shortcut.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Extremal:** look at the largest, smallest, first or last object of the relevant kind and show it has the property.
- **Pigeonhole:** count objects and boxes. More objects than boxes forces a collision; the collision is often the answer (equal prefix sums mod $m$, a repeated value).
- **Halving:** if you can prove "an answer exists in this half", you can binary search even on an unsorted array.
:::

**Complexity.** Typically turns an $O(n)$ scan into $O(\log n)$, or a search into an immediate "yes".

{{< include ../problems/lc-0162-find-peak-element/problem.qmd >}}

[**From walking uphill to counting.** Find Peak argues by walking to an extreme. Find the Duplicate counts instead: too many values in too few boxes forces a repeat, and the same count says which half of the value range holds it.]{.flow-bridge}


### Find the duplicate: pigeonhole on the values {#sec-pf-p4-duplicate}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0287-find-the-duplicate-number/card.qmd >}}

The graph chapter solves this problem in full with the cycle argument. The pigeonhole gives a second, slower solution that needs no graph at all, and it is the cleanest example of **halving by an existence proof**. There are $n + 1$ values in the $n$ boxes $1..n$, so a duplicate exists. Better: if more than $mid$ values lie in $[1, mid]$, those $mid$ boxes hold too many values, so a duplicate lies in $[1, mid]$.

**Invariant.** Keep a value range $[lo, hi]$ such that the array has **more than $hi - lo + 1$ elements with values in $[lo, hi]$**. Initially $[1, n]$ holds all $n + 1$ elements. Count the elements in $[lo, mid]$: if there are more than $mid - lo + 1$, the left half keeps the invariant; otherwise the right half must hold more than its size, so it keeps the invariant. When $lo = hi$, one box holds at least two values: $lo$ is the duplicate. Each round is one full pass, so the cost is $O(n \log n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

```{python}
#| label: pf-duplicate
def find_duplicate_bs(a):
    lo, hi = 1, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        inside = sum(lo <= x <= mid for x in a)
        assert sum(lo <= x <= hi for x in a) > hi - lo + 1        # the invariant
        if inside > mid - lo + 1:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

for _ in range(1000):
    n = random.randint(1, 15)
    d = random.randint(1, n)
    rest = random.sample([v for v in range(1, n + 1) if v != d], random.randint(0, n - 1))
    a = rest + [d] * (n + 1 - len(rest))          # d repeated, total length n + 1
    random.shuffle(a)
    assert find_duplicate_bs(a) == d

assert find_duplicate_bs([1, 3, 4, 2, 2]) == 2 and find_duplicate_bs([3, 3, 3, 3, 3]) == 3
```

[**From a search to a shortcut.** In Find the Duplicate the pigeonhole guides a binary search. In Modulo Sum it ends the problem outright: once $n \ge m$ the answer is always yes, and only small $n$ needs real work.]{.flow-bridge}


{{< include ../problems/cf-577b-modulo-sum/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 5: lower bounds and adversary arguments {#sec-pf-p5}

**From one algorithm to all of them.** Every proof so far was about the algorithm in front of us. A lower bound is a claim about every possible algorithm, so the argument changes: count the outcomes the algorithm must tell apart, or let an adversary answer each question as unhelpfully as it can.

**Recognise it.** "Can you do better?", a limit on the number of queries in an interactive problem, or a problem that asks for an exact number of comparisons.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
1. Fix the model: which operations count (comparisons, queries, probes).
2. **Counting bound:** if the algorithm must distinguish $L$ outcomes and each operation has $k$ possible answers, it needs $\lceil \log_k L \rceil$ operations.
3. **Adversary bound:** define what the algorithm must "learn" (units of information), show each operation can reveal only a few units when the adversary answers cleverly, and divide.
4. Look for an algorithm that meets the bound exactly; if it does, both are optimal.
:::

**Complexity.** These problems are about exact operation counts, not just asymptotics.

{{< include ../problems/cf-730b-minimum-and-maximum/problem.qmd >}}

[**From two answers to a runner-up.** Min and max share comparisons by pairing elements. The second largest must have lost directly to the largest, so a knockout tournament records who beat whom and searches only the $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ elements that lost to the winner.]{.flow-bridge}


### Problem: Second largest in $n + \lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 2$ comparisons {#sec-pf-p5-second}

::: {.p-statement}
Find the second-largest of $n$ distinct numbers using as few comparisons as possible, and prove your count is optimal. (A classic interview question; no judge needed.)
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Run a knockout tournament: $n - 1$ comparisons find the maximum. The second largest lost **only** to the maximum (it beats everyone else), so it is among the at most $\lceil \log_2 n\rceil$ players the champion beat. A second, small tournament among them costs at most $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 1$ more.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. Pair players up round by round (an odd player out gets a bye); record for each winner the list of players it beat. The champion plays at most one game per round: $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ games.
2. Take the maximum of the champion's beaten list.

**Lower bound sketch.** Every element except the maximum must lose a comparison ($n - 1$ comparisons). Among the $k$ elements that lost directly to the maximum, all except the second largest must **also** lose to someone else, or they could be second. So at least $n - 1 + k - 1$ comparisons. An adversary can force $k \ge \lceil\log_2 n\rceil$: it gives each element a weight (initially 1); when two elements meet, the heavier wins and absorbs the loser's weight. Weights at most double per game, and the champion ends with weight $n$, so it must have played at least $\log_2 n$ games. Hence $n + \lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 2$ is optimal (Kislitsyn, 1964; Knuth vol. 3 §5.3.3).
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
#### Python

```{python}
#| label: pf-second
def second_largest(a):
    comparisons = 0
    players = [(x, []) for x in a]          # (value, values it has beaten)
    while len(players) > 1:
        nxt = []
        for i in range(0, len(players) - 1, 2):
            (x, bx), (y, by) = players[i], players[i + 1]
            comparisons += 1
            nxt.append((x, bx + [y]) if x > y else (y, by + [x]))
        if len(players) % 2:
            nxt.append(players[-1])          # bye
        players = nxt
    beaten = players[0][1]
    best = beaten[0]
    for v in beaten[1:]:
        comparisons += 1
        best = max(best, v)
    return best, comparisons

for _ in range(2000):
    n = random.randint(2, 70)
    a = random.sample(range(1000), n)
    second, c = second_largest(a)
    assert second == sorted(a)[-2]
    assert c <= n + math.ceil(math.log2(n)) - 2
assert second_largest(list(range(64)))[1] == 64 + 6 - 2
```

#### C++

```cpp
int secondLargest(const vector<int>& a) {
    vector<pair<int, vector<int>>> p;
    for (int x : a) p.push_back({x, {}});
    while (p.size() > 1) {
        vector<pair<int, vector<int>>> nxt;
        for (size_t i = 0; i + 1 < p.size(); i += 2) {
            auto& [x, bx] = p[i]; auto& [y, by] = p[i + 1];
            if (x > y) { bx.push_back(y); nxt.push_back(move(p[i])); }
            else       { by.push_back(x); nxt.push_back(move(p[i + 1])); }
        }
        if (p.size() % 2) nxt.push_back(move(p.back()));
        p.swap(nxt);
    }
    return *max_element(p[0].second.begin(), p[0].second.end());
}
```
:::

::: {#fig-pf-tournament}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
vals = [5, 2, 6, 9, 7, 1, 8, 4]
assert second_largest(vals) == (8, 9)
def build(vals):
    level = [V.Node(str(v), color="muted") for v in vals]
    while len(level) > 1:
        level = [V.Node(str(max(int(a_.label), int(b_.label))), [a_, b_], color="indigo")
                 for a_, b_ in zip(level[::2], level[1::2])]
    return level[0]
def mark(v, champ):
    if not v.children:
        return
    a_, b_ = v.children
    win, lose = (a_, b_) if int(a_.label) == champ else (b_, a_)
    if v.label == str(champ):
        v.color = "green"
        lose.color = "amber"
        mark(win, champ)
def draw(ax, p):
    root = build(vals)
    mark(root, 9)
    def paint_leaf(v):
        for c in v.children:
            paint_leaf(c)
        if not v.children and v.label == "9":
            v.color = "green"
    paint_leaf(root)
    V.tree(ax, p, root, dx=1.1, dy=1.3)
V.show(draw)
```

A knockout tournament on 8 values. The champion 9 beat only 6, 5 and 8 (amber) on its way up, so the second largest is among those three: 7 + 2 = 9 comparisons, n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Comparisons** at most $n + \lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 2$ (optimal). **Time** $O(n)$ overall, since the beaten lists have total length $n - 1$. **Space** $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 2$: one comparison.
- With duplicates, define "second largest" first (second distinct value, or second position?); the tournament returns the second **position**, which may equal the maximum.
- "Sort and take the second" costs $O(n\log n)$; two linear passes cost $2n - 3$. Both are correct but not optimal, which is the point of the question.
:::

- [LC 414 · Third Maximum Number](https://leetcode.com/problems/third-maximum-number/){difficulty="Easy"}
:::

## Pattern 6: invariants and monovariants of a process {#sec-pf-p6}

**From one run to a process.** The last kind of claim is about a process that can run in many orders: apply moves until you are stuck, or try to reach a target. Find a quantity the moves never change (an invariant) or always change in one direction (a monovariant), and what is reachable follows.

**Recognise it.** "Apply operations any number of times; can you reach the target?" or "what is the minimum cost to make all equal?", where operations are local and the state space is huge.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
1. Simulate a few operations by hand (or by BFS on tiny inputs) and look for what **does not change**: a parity, a sum mod $k$, the gcd, the multiset of differences, the endpoints.
2. Prove the quantity is invariant under every operation: target with a different value is unreachable.
3. Prove the converse: when the invariant matches, construct the sequence of operations (often the hard half).
4. For termination or cost, find a monovariant that moves one way.
:::

**Complexity.** The invariant check is usually $O(n)$ or $O(n\log n)$, versus an exponential search.

{{< include ../problems/lc-1217-minimum-cost-to-move-chips-to-the-same-position/problem.qmd >}}

[**From one number per item to a multiset.** In the chips problem the invariant is one number per chip, its parity. In Magic Stones an operation swaps two adjacent differences, so the invariant is the whole multiset of differences, plus the two end stones.]{.flow-bridge}


{{< include ../problems/cf-1110e-magic-stones/problem.qmd >}}

**Looking back.** Each pattern made the same move at a larger scale: name a quantity, then show what happens to it. For a loop it is an invariant, for a recursion a claim about $n$, for a greedy the distance to an optimal solution, for existence a count, for a lower bound the information still missing, and for a process a value the moves cannot change.

## Pattern map

| Signal | Technique | Section |
|---|---|---|
| A loop whose correctness is not obvious | Loop invariant + variant | @sec-pf-p1 |
| Binary search that may not terminate | Variant $hi - lo$ must shrink; round `mid` correctly | @sec-pf-invariants |
| "One pass, keep a candidate" | Invariant on the processed prefix | @sec-pf-p1-majority |
| Recursive or DP solution | Strong induction on size / state order | @sec-pf-induction |
| Two-player game on a number | Brute-force table, guess pattern, prove by induction | @sec-pf-p2 |
| "Sort by some key, then take greedily" | Test against brute force; exchange or stays ahead | @sec-pf-p3 |
| "Some element with property X exists" | Extremal principle | @sec-pf-p4-peak |
| More items than possible values / residues | Pigeonhole | @sec-pf-p4-duplicate, @sec-pf-p4-modulo |
| "Can you do better?", query limits | Decision tree, adversary | @sec-pf-p5 |
| "Apply operations; can you reach the target?" | Invariant of the process | @sec-pf-p6 |
| "Does this process stop?" | Monovariant | @sec-pf-process |

## Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Checking an invariant only on the "happy" branch.** Maintenance must hold for every branch of the loop body.
- **Forgetting termination.** A binary search with `lo = mid` and `mid` rounded down loops forever on two elements.
- **Induction that fails at the smallest case** (the "horses" error), or that uses $P(n-1)$ when the recursion calls a different size.
- **"Proving" a greedy by examples.** Samples are not proofs; run a brute-force comparison on hundreds of small random inputs.
- **Exchange arguments that break feasibility.** After the swap, check that the modified solution still satisfies every constraint (capacity, counts per city, non-overlap).
- **Applying Boyer–Moore without the majority guarantee** — verify with a second pass.
- **Lower bounds in the wrong model.** $\Omega(n\log n)$ is for comparison sorting; counting sort and hashing are not bound by it.
- **Proving only one direction** of an invariant argument: "invariant differs ⇒ unreachable" is easy; "invariant equal ⇒ reachable" needs a construction.
:::

## Exercises

**1. [E]** State a loop invariant for "find the maximum of an array" and use it to prove the loop correct.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Loop `best = a[0]; for i in 1..n-1: best = max(best, a[i])`. Invariant at the top of iteration $i$: `best` $= \max(a_0, \dots, a_{i-1})$. Initialisation: $i = 1$, `best` $= a_0$. Maintenance: $\max(\max(a_0..a_{i-1}), a_i) = \max(a_0..a_i)$. Termination: $i = n$, so `best` is the maximum of the whole array.
:::

**2. [E]** Prove by structural induction that a binary tree with $n$ nodes has exactly $n + 1$ empty (null) child pointers.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Empty tree: $n = 0$ and it is one null pointer. ✓ A tree with root and subtrees of sizes $n_L$, $n_R$ ($n = n_L + n_R + 1$) has $(n_L + 1) + (n_R + 1) = n + 1$ null pointers by the hypothesis on the subtrees. ✓
:::

**3. [E]** Prove that subtractive Euclid (`while a != b: if a > b: a -= b else: b -= a`, with $a, b \ge 1$) terminates, and say what it returns.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Variant: $a + b$, a positive integer that strictly decreases each step (we subtract a positive number), so the loop stops. Invariant: $\gcd(a, b)$ is unchanged, since $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(a - b, b)$. At exit $a = b$, and $\gcd(a, a) = a$, so it returns the gcd. It can take $\Theta(\max(a,b))$ steps (e.g. $a = 10^9$, $b = 1$), unlike the modulo version.
:::

**4. [E]** Give a loop invariant for selection sort.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At the top of iteration $i$: $a[0..i)$ is sorted, and every element of $a[0..i)$ is $\le$ every element of $a[i..n)$. Selecting the minimum of $a[i..n)$ and swapping it to position $i$ maintains both. At $i = n$, the whole array is sorted. Note the second clause: "$a[0..i)$ is sorted" alone is not enough to conclude anything about later positions.
:::

**5. [E]** In the game where players take 1 to $k$ stones (last stone wins), prove that the first player loses iff $(k+1) \mid n$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Same induction as Nim (@sec-pf-p2-nim): from a multiple of $k+1$ every move lands on a non-multiple; from a non-multiple, taking $n \bmod (k+1)$ stones lands on a multiple. Base: $n = 0$ is lost for the player to move.
:::

**6. [M] (coding)** For activity selection, find counterexamples for the greedy keys "earliest start" and "shortest duration" by random search.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
def keep_greedy(intervals, key):
    chosen = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=key):
        if all(e <= cs or s >= ce for cs, ce in chosen):
            chosen.append((s, e))
    return len(chosen)

def keep_opt(intervals):
    return len(intervals) - erase_overlap_brute(intervals)

def find_counterexample(key, tries=20000):
    for _ in range(tries):
        iv = random_intervals(random.randint(2, 4))
        if keep_greedy(iv, key) < keep_opt(iv):
            return sorted(iv)

by_start = find_counterexample(lambda iv: iv[0])
by_length = find_counterexample(lambda iv: iv[1] - iv[0])
print("by start :", by_start)
print("by length:", by_length)
assert by_start and by_length
assert find_counterexample(lambda iv: iv[1], tries=5000) is None   # by end: never fails
```
"Fewest conflicts first" also fails, but its smallest counterexample has 11 intervals (Kleinberg–Tardos, Fig. 4.1), which random search on 4 intervals will not find — a reminder that "no counterexample found" is evidence, not proof.
:::

**7. [M]** Prove that the fractional knapsack is solved by taking items in decreasing order of value per weight, and show this greedy fails for 0/1 knapsack.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Exchange: suppose an optimal solution takes less of item $i$ and more of item $j$ than greedy, with $v_i/w_i > v_j/w_j$. Move $\varepsilon$ weight from $j$ to $i$: the value changes by $\varepsilon(v_i/w_i - v_j/w_j) > 0$, contradicting optimality. 0/1 counterexample: capacity 50, items (value 60, weight 10), (100, 20), (120, 30). Greedy by ratio takes the first two (value 160) and cannot fit the third; the optimum takes the last two (220).
:::

**8. [M]** Prove that in any group of $n \ge 2$ people, two have the same number of friends inside the group (friendship is symmetric).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Degrees lie in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: $n$ values for $n$ people. But 0 and $n-1$ cannot both occur (someone friends with everyone means nobody has 0 friends). So the degrees lie in a set of $n - 1$ values, and by pigeonhole two people share a degree.
:::

**9. [M]** Prove that any comparison algorithm that finds the maximum of $n$ distinct numbers needs at least $n - 1$ comparisons.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Suppose it uses fewer. The comparisons form a graph on $n$ vertices with fewer than $n - 1$ edges, so it is disconnected. Take the component not containing the reported maximum, and add a huge constant to all its values: every comparison answer is unchanged (comparisons inside the component keep their order; there are no comparisons across components), but now the true maximum is in that component. The algorithm gives the same (now wrong) output. Contradiction.
:::

**10. [M] (coding)** Scheduling jobs with processing times $p_i$ on one machine, minimise the sum of completion times. Prove that sorting by $p_i$ (shortest first) is optimal and check it against all permutations.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Adjacent exchange: if job $j$ runs immediately before job $i$ with $p_j > p_i$, swapping them leaves every other completion time unchanged, and changes the pair's contribution from $(T + p_j) + (T + p_j + p_i)$ to $(T + p_i) + (T + p_i + p_j)$, a decrease of $p_j - p_i > 0$. So an optimal order has no such inversion: it is sorted.

```{python}
def total_completion(order):
    t = total = 0
    for p in order:
        t += p
        total += t
    return total

for _ in range(300):
    p = [random.randint(1, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 6))]
    assert total_completion(sorted(p)) == min(total_completion(q) for q in permutations(p))
```
:::

**11. [M] (coding)** With weights $w_i > 0$, minimise $\sum w_i C_i$ (weighted completion times). Show that sorting by $p_i / w_i$ (Smith's rule) is optimal.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Swapping adjacent $j$ (first) and $i$ changes the objective by $w_j p_i - w_i p_j$. This is negative (an improvement) exactly when $p_i / w_i < p_j / w_j$. So any optimal order is sorted by $p/w$. Compare with cross-multiplication to avoid floating point.

```{python}
from functools import cmp_to_key

def weighted_total(order):
    t = total = 0
    for p, w in order:
        t += p
        total += w * t
    return total

def smith(jobs):
    return sorted(jobs, key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: a[0] * b[1] - b[0] * a[1]))

for _ in range(300):
    jobs = [(random.randint(1, 9), random.randint(1, 9)) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 6))]
    assert weighted_total(smith(jobs)) == min(weighted_total(q) for q in permutations(jobs))
```
:::

**12. [M]** Prove that Kadane's algorithm (@sec-cx-p1-max-subarray) is correct.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Invariant after processing $a_0..a_i$: `cur` $= e_i$ (best sum of a subarray **ending** at $i$) and `best` $= \max_{j\le i} e_j$. Maintenance: a subarray ending at $i+1$ is either $[a_{i+1}]$ or a subarray ending at $i$ extended by $a_{i+1}$, so $e_{i+1} = a_{i+1} + \max(e_i, 0)$. Termination: every subarray ends at some index, so the maximum over all $e_j$ is the answer. Note the induction is on the **stronger** quantity $e_i$, not on the answer itself (strengthening the hypothesis).
:::

**13. [H]** Prove the Erdős–Szekeres theorem: any sequence of $rs + 1$ distinct numbers has an increasing subsequence of length $r + 1$ or a decreasing subsequence of length $s + 1$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Label each position $i$ with $(u_i, d_i)$: the lengths of the longest increasing and decreasing subsequences **ending** at $i$. For $i < j$: if $a_i < a_j$ then $u_j > u_i$; if $a_i > a_j$ then $d_j > d_i$. So all labels are distinct. If $u_i \le r$ and $d_i \le s$ for all $i$, there are at most $rs$ distinct labels for $rs + 1$ positions — pigeonhole contradiction.
:::

**14. [H]** Prove that merging two sorted lists of $n$ elements each needs $2n - 1$ comparisons in the worst case.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Adversary: let the answer be the interleaving $a_1 < b_1 < a_2 < b_2 < \dots < a_n < b_n$. Each adjacent pair in this order ($a_i, b_i$ and $b_i, a_{i+1}$; $2n - 1$ pairs) must be compared directly: if, say, $b_i$ and $a_{i+1}$ were never compared, swapping their values gives another input consistent with all answers but with a different merged order. So $2n - 1$ comparisons, which the standard merge achieves.
:::

**15. [H] (coding)** Starting from the pair $(1, 1)$, a move replaces $(a, b)$ by $(a + b, b)$ or $(a, a + b)$. Prove that $(x, y)$ is reachable iff $\gcd(x, y) = 1$, and check by BFS.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Invariant: $\gcd(a + b, b) = \gcd(a, b)$, so the gcd stays 1: pairs with gcd $> 1$ are unreachable. Converse by strong induction on $x + y$: if $\gcd(x, y) = 1$ and $(x, y) \ne (1,1)$, then $x \ne y$ (else both are 1); say $x > y$. Then $(x - y, y)$ has gcd 1 and smaller sum, so it is reachable, and one move gives $(x, y)$. This is subtractive Euclid run backwards.

```{python}
N = 30
reach, q = {(1, 1)}, deque([(1, 1)])
while q:
    a, b = q.popleft()
    for nxt in ((a + b, b), (a, a + b)):
        if max(nxt) <= N and nxt not in reach:
            reach.add(nxt); q.append(nxt)
assert all(((x, y) in reach) == (math.gcd(x, y) == 1) for x in range(1, N + 1) for y in range(1, N + 1))
```
:::

**16. [H] (coding)** The numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ are written on a board. A move erases two numbers $a, b$ and writes $|a - b|$. After $n - 1$ moves one number remains. Prove its parity is always that of $n(n+1)/2$, and check exhaustively for $n \le 7$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a + b$ and $|a - b|$ have the same parity, so the parity of the total sum is invariant. Initially the sum is $n(n+1)/2$; at the end it is the single remaining number.

```{python}
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def finals(state):
    if len(state) == 1:
        return frozenset(state)
    out = set()
    for i, j in combinations(range(len(state)), 2):
        rest = state[:i] + state[i + 1 : j] + state[j + 1 :]
        out |= finals(tuple(sorted(rest + (abs(state[i] - state[j]),))))
    return frozenset(out)

for n in range(1, 8):
    assert {v % 2 for v in finals(tuple(range(1, n + 1)))} == {n * (n + 1) // 2 % 2}
```
:::

## Interview questions

**1. What is a loop invariant? Give one for binary search.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A statement true before every iteration; it plus the exit condition gives the result. For lower-bound binary search on $[lo, hi)$: all elements before $lo$ are $< x$ and all from $hi$ on are $\ge x$. At exit $lo = hi$ is the answer. The variant $hi - lo$ halves, giving $O(\log n)$ and termination.
:::

**2. How do you convince an interviewer that your greedy algorithm is correct?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Name the greedy choice and give an exchange argument: "take any optimal solution; if its first choice differs from mine, swap it for mine; the result is still valid and no worse; repeat". Or "greedy stays ahead": after every step greedy is at least as good by some measure. Then mention you would also check it against brute force on small inputs.
:::

**3. Your greedy passes all samples. How do you gain more confidence before submitting?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write a brute force (try all subsets or permutations), generate many small random inputs (sizes 1–8, small values to force ties), and compare. Small inputs find counterexamples fastest, and once found, the smallest one usually explains why the idea fails. This takes five minutes and catches most wrong greedies.
:::

**4. Why can comparison sorts not beat $O(n\log n)$, and how do counting sort and radix sort get around it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A comparison sort is a binary decision tree with at least $n!$ leaves, so its height is at least $\log_2 n! = \Theta(n\log n)$. Counting and radix sort do not compare elements: they use values as array indices, which gives more than two outcomes per operation, so the decision-tree bound does not apply. They pay instead with a dependence on the value range or the number of digits.
:::

**5. Can you find the minimum and maximum with fewer than $2n - 2$ comparisons? Is your answer optimal?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Yes: compare elements in pairs, then the smaller against the current min and the larger against the current max: $\lceil 3n/2\rceil - 2$ comparisons. An adversary argument shows this is optimal: $2n - 2$ units of information are needed and only comparisons between two fresh elements give two units.
:::

**6. What is the difference between partial and total correctness? How do you prove a loop terminates?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Partial: if it stops, the answer is right. Total: also, it always stops. Termination: exhibit a variant, a non-negative integer that strictly decreases each iteration (such as $hi - lo$, the number of unprocessed elements, or $a + b$ in subtractive gcd).
:::

**7. What is optimal substructure? Give a problem where it fails.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems, so a DP or greedy can build it from them. Shortest paths have it (a subpath of a shortest path is shortest). **Longest simple path** does not: the longest simple path from $u$ to $w$ through $v$ need not consist of longest simple paths $u \to v$ and $v \to w$, because those may share vertices. Longest simple path is NP-hard.
:::

**8. Does Boyer–Moore voting work if there is no majority element?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It returns *some* candidate, which may not be a majority (e.g. $[1, 2, 3]$ returns 3). The invariant only guarantees that **if** a majority exists, it is the candidate. Verify with a second counting pass. Space stays $O(1)$, time $O(n)$.
:::

**9. Why does "binary search on the answer" work?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It needs a monotone predicate: if $P(x)$ holds then $P(y)$ holds for all $y \ge x$ (e.g. "can we finish with capacity $x$?"). Then the set of good $x$ is a suffix, and binary search finds its first element with the invariant "$P(lo-1)$ false, $P(hi)$ true". Without monotonicity the search can skip over the answer.
:::

**10. What is the extremal principle? Give an algorithmic example.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Consider an object that is maximal or minimal in some sense and show it has the needed property. Examples: the first vertex of a longest path in a DAG has in-degree 0 (so topological sort can start); the global maximum of an array is a peak; the interval that ends first can be in an optimal schedule.
:::

**11. Find the second largest of $n$ numbers. How many comparisons do you need?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A tournament finds the maximum in $n - 1$; the second largest lost only to the champion, so it is among the $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ players the champion beat: $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 1$ more comparisons. Total $n + \lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 2$, which is optimal by an adversary argument. Two passes ($2n - 3$) or sorting are correct but use more comparisons.
:::

**12. What is an adversary argument?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A lower-bound technique: an adversary answers the algorithm's queries on the fly, consistent with at least one input, choosing answers that reveal as little as possible. If the adversary can keep two inputs with different answers alive for $g(n)$ queries, any algorithm needs $g(n)$ queries in the worst case. Used for min-max, second largest, merging, and query limits in interactive problems.
:::

**13. Why is Kruskal's algorithm correct?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cut property (an exchange argument): for any cut, the lightest edge crossing it is in some MST. Kruskal adds the lightest edge that joins two different components, which is the lightest edge across the cut separating one of those components from the rest. If an MST $T$ lacks it, adding it to $T$ creates a cycle that crosses the cut again through some heavier-or-equal edge; swapping gives a spanning tree no heavier. More generally, forests form a matroid, and greedy is optimal on matroids.
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **Loop:** invariant (initialisation, maintenance, termination) + variant for termination.
- **Recursion/DP:** strong induction on size or state order; trust the recursive calls.
- **Greedy:** exchange (swap the first difference) or stays ahead (induction on steps); always test against brute force.
- **Existence:** extremal element, or pigeonhole (more items than boxes).
- **Lower bounds:** $\lceil\log_2(\#\text{outcomes})\rceil$; adversary for exact counts ($\lceil 3n/2\rceil - 2$ min-max, $n + \lceil\log_2 n\rceil - 2$ second largest).
- **Processes:** invariant ⇒ impossibility; monovariant ⇒ termination.
:::

- A proof sketch of three sentences — invariant, why it is maintained, why it gives the answer — is what interviewers want.
- The invariant is usually the postcondition with one quantity relaxed.
- A loop that terminates needs a variant; binary search bugs are variant bugs.
- Strengthen the hypothesis when the plain claim does not carry through the induction.
- Find patterns in games and processes with a brute-force table, then prove them.
- Greedy correctness is the exception, not the rule; prove it or break it.
- Pigeonhole and extremal arguments often turn into $O(1)$ shortcuts or binary searches.
- Lower bounds tell you when to stop optimising; they depend on the model.

## Further reading

- **CLRS**, *Introduction to Algorithms*, 4th ed. — [MIT Press](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262046305/introduction-to-algorithms/): §2.1 loop invariants, ch. 15 greedy proofs, §8.1 sorting lower bounds, §9.1 minimum and maximum; 3rd ed. §16.4 matroids.
- **Erickson**, *Algorithms* — [free online text](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/): ch. 1 induction and recursion, ch. 4 greedy proofs ("greedy stays ahead").
- **Kleinberg and Tardos**, *Algorithm Design* — [Pearson](https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/algorithm-design/P200000003259/9780137546350): ch. 4, the clearest treatment of "greedy stays ahead" and exchange arguments.
- **Knuth**, *TAOCP* vol. 3, §5.3.3 — [The Art of Computer Programming](https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html): selection lower bounds, including the second-largest bound (Kislitsyn).
- **Gries**, *The Science of Programming* (1981) — [Springer](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4612-5983-1): loop invariants as a way to *derive* programs, not just check them.
- **Engel**, *Problem-Solving Strategies* — [Springer](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b97682), ch. 1–2: invariants, monovariants and the extremal principle, with many olympiad problems.
